items.topic: Bad debts and provisions on debtors
items.question: Trial balance, 31 March 2026: Debtors ₹5,20,000; Bad debts already written off ₹6,000; Provision for doubtful debts ₹18,000; Provision for discount on debtors ₹7,000. Further bad debts ₹20,000 to be written off. Required: doubtful debts provision 5%, then discount provision 2% on remaining good debtors. Total charge to P&L?
items.explanation: Debtors after write-off ₹5,00,000. Doubtful provision 5% = ₹25,000. Discount provision is 2% on ₹4,75,000 = ₹9,500. Closing provisions ₹34,500 less opening ₹25,000 = ₹9,500. Add bad debts ₹26,000 = ₹35,500.

why_not.C: Charged discount provision on ₹5,00,000 without deducting doubtful debts provision.
why_not.D: Left out the ₹6,000 bad debts already written off in the trial balance.
why_not.B: Forgot the ₹20,000 further bad debts adjustment.

items.exam_tip: Discount provision is made on good debtors: deduct bad debts and doubtful provision first. Add bad debts already in the trial balance.
items.calculation:
debtors = 520000 - 20000
pdd = debtors * 5 / 100
pdisc = (debtors - pdd) * 2 / 100
closing = pdd + pdisc
opening = 18000 + 7000
bad = 6000 + 20000
answer = bad + closing - opening
check_notes: Checker: The wording 'Total charge to P&L' could be read as excluding the ₹6,000 already written off. That reading gives ₹29,500, which is option D. The question should say that total bad debts, including those already in the trial balance, are charged.

Checker: The discount provision is labelled 'provision for discount on debtors', which is standard. The question should say explicitly that the 2% applies after deducting the new doubtful debts provision.

items.question: A project needs ₹10,00,000 for machinery and ₹2,00,000 working capital, both at time 0. Annual net cash inflow is ₹3,00,000 for 5 years. At year 5 end, scrap ₹1,00,000 is realised and working capital is recovered. At 10% (annuity factor 3.79, year-5 factor 0.62), NPV is:
items.explanation: Working capital is an outflow at time 0 and is recovered at year 5 end, so it is discounted. Scrap is also a year-5 inflow. NPV = PV of inflows ₹13,23,000 less outlay ₹12,00,000.

why_not.A: Ignores working capital completely, both the outlay and its recovery.
why_not.C: Takes the year-5 scrap and WC recovery at full value without discounting.
why_not.D: Treats WC as outflow but forgets to add its recovery; only scrap is counted.

items.exam_tip: Working capital goes out at time 0 and comes back at project end; discount the recovery like any other year-end inflow.
items.calculation:
pv_annuity = 300000*3.79
pv_end = (100000+200000)*0.62
outlay = 1000000+200000
answer = pv_annuity + pv_end - outlay
items.reviewer_note: Scrap assumed pre-tax/no tax effect; annual inflow stated as net cash inflow.
check_notes: Writer: Scrap assumed pre-tax/no tax effect; annual inflow stated as net cash inflow.

items.question: An importer buys USD under a 3-month OTC forward with a bank. Another importer buys USD futures of the same maturity on an exchange. The rupee weakens steadily for both. Which statement is correct?
options: Futures loss is paid daily through margin; forward loss falls due only at maturity
Forward loss is paid daily through margin; futures loss falls due only at maturity
Clearing house absorbs the futures loss, so the futures buyer pays no margin
Both carry equal default risk, as each contract has one counterparty
items.explanation: Futures are marked to market daily, so losses are settled through the margin account each day. A forward is usually settled only at maturity, so the bank carries credit exposure until then. The clearing house guarantees futures.

why_not.B: Reverses the two: the daily mark-to-market feature belongs to futures, not OTC forwards.
why_not.C: Clearing house guarantees performance; it does not bear losses and margin is still required.
why_not.D: Futures counterparty is the clearing house, so default risk is much lower than in a forward.

items.exam_tip: Futures: daily settlement and clearing house guarantee. Forward: settle at maturity and counterparty risk.
check_notes: Checker: The scenario is internally inconsistent. An importer who buys USD gains when the rupee weakens, since USD appreciates. Both importers would have gains, not losses. Options A and B talk about 'loss'.
Checker: A would be cleaner as 'The rupee strengthens steadily' or as 'mark-to-market gains/losses are settled daily'.
Checker: 'Forward loss falls due only at maturity' assumes a standard OTC forward with no collateral or CSA. This is usual, but it isn't stated.
Checker: The key is still unambiguous.
